body:
_This is the final article in a three-part series on the risks of private credit.__Part 1__described private credit and highlighted the risks to retail investors in private credit funds structured as nontraded business development companies.__Part 2__widened the lens to private credit funds generally, identifying risks to retirement savers, to those who hold retirement annuities and insurance policies, and to the financial system. This article recommends steps that Congress and regulators can take to reduce the risks of private credit._

The United States’ recent financial history teaches that regulators should do more to detect and address the buildup of risk early, rather than waiting for a crisis to occur. There are many steps that Congress and regulators should take to better detect growing risk in private credit funds and business development companies (BDCs) and to protect the financial system and its participants, including Americans who contribute to an employer-sponsored pension or a 401(k) plan, hold a retirement annuity or insurance policy from an insurance company, or deposit their money in a traditional bank.

Private credit and other private investments—also known as alternative investments—should be excluded from, or remain an extremely limited option for, most 401(k) plans. And investment plan managers and advisers should remain fully liable for any breach of fiduciary duties, without the safe harbor that the Trump administration has proposed.

Employer-provided retirement saving plans receive special tax treatment under Internal Revenue Code Section 401(k) and were created in order to promote the public policy of encouraging Americans to save for their retirement. Wages deposited in a 401(k) are not taxed until they are distributed to the employee at retirement, and employers also receive tax benefits, such as a deduction for providing matching contributions to their employees’ 401(k)s. Thus, 401(k)s provide taxpayer-subsidized benefits to both workers and their employers as the federal government forgoes taxes that otherwise would have funded other government programs and expenses.

Congress expressly created BDCs to facilitate investment of capital in private small and midsize companies, including by retail investors. As of the second quarter of 2026, nearly 10 percent of debt investments by the largest BDCs were associated with distressed borrowers, and the valuations of loans to their portfolio companies have been questioned by banks, investment firms, and others. Thus, investments in BDCs are typically high-risk and not appropriate for most 401(k) plans. Other private credit funds, as well as private equity funds and other private assets, are not fully transparent and by definition are not publicly traded; thus, they are not subject to market discipline. Allowing any of these high-risk investments in 401(k)s could end up squandering taxpayer dollars by introducing unjustified risks into taxpayer-subsidized savings and undermining the financial security of Americans’ retirement savings.

When shares of private credit funds are offered to ordinary investors, whether accredited, suitable under state law, or neither, the funds should provide full and fair disclosure to those investors. Such disclosures should include more granular and verifiable detail about the valuations of companies to which private credit funds loan, along with supporting data and data on the number, industry, and financial condition of companies in their portfolios. Disclosures should also include full disclosure of fees, including incentive fees, charged to investors, since such fees can consume returns. Any restrictions on redemption of shares should also be clearly disclosed and explained to investors.

While the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) requires publicly traded and even nontraded BDCs to make many of these disclosures, it does not require the same of private BDCs and other private credit funds. Yet the latter may take advantage of Regulation D or other securities offering exemptions to offer shares to ordinary investors, some of whom may not even qualify as accredited investors, without having to publicly register the offering or file public reports. But they should have to comply with public registration and disclosure rules when they offer shares to ordinary investors, even those who qualify as accredited. One way to do that may be to require all private credit funds to comply with the filing requirements of Form N-2, just as public BDCs do, whenever they are offering shares to ordinary investors. Alternatively, it would be reasonable to prohibit these other private credit funds from offering shares to ordinary investors entirely, since the lack of public trading of these funds’ shares, even with such disclosures, prevents the kind of price discovery upon which ordinary investors normally rely.

Where insurance companies are concerned, state insurance regulators could require the public disclosure of private credit ratings on which insurance companies’ capital requirements are based, thereby leveraging the collective knowledge of the market to assess valuations of the portfolios of the private credit funds in which those insurance companies invest.

Disclosures are the cornerstone of U.S. securities laws. The Securities Act of 1933 requires companies offering securities to the public to provide full and fair disclosure about the securities as well as the risks associated with investing in them. Likewise, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 requires ongoing periodic reporting by companies with securities trading in public markets. This market transparency helps investors make sound investment decisions, enables other market participants to price risk, and helps public authorities police securities fraud.

The default of certain private credit portfolio companies in 2025 precipitated investor concerns about the quality of their private credit investments, including whether valuations put forth by private credit funds were reliable and whether the funds had conducted adequate due diligence. Concerns have also arisen about the future of private credit fund loans to software companies in light of the threats these software companies face due to rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI). These concerns are compounded by the fact that many loans to software companies are coming due between now and 2029 and will need to be refinanced.

Managers of pension funds, managers and trustees of 401(k) plans and the consultants they hire, and the investment officers of insurance companies all qualify as accredited investors, but Congress should recognize that they all need adequate information to make sound decisions and that those decisions affect the millions of Americans who entrust their savings to them. Congress should also note that in some instances investment advisers’ strategies may pose risks to participants in the retirement plans they manage or to retirees whose annuities they manage. As the private credit market grows and pension funds and insurance companies invest more intensely in these funds, transparency is needed to ensure that investment decisions involving the savings of average Americans are protected from lack of transparency and the risks it can hide.

Given the complexity and interconnectedness of today’s financial system and the growth of largely opaque private markets, it is increasingly difficult for financial regulators to monitor the web of credit risk in the financial system. Both traditional banks and private credit funds should be accountable for providing information that financial regulators need to monitor those risks.

One source that financial regulators use to assess risk in the financial system is banks’ quarterly call reports. Banks should be required to provide more detail on the private credit funds to which they loan, including information about the loan portfolios of those funds and any other direct or indirect linkages the bank has to private credit funds, including loans that the bank may have to the funds’ major investors.

To assist banking regulators in carrying out their statutory duties, Congress should require private credit funds (including BDCs) to confidentially report on a quarterly basis to the Federal Reserve information needed to assess risks to regulated banks and to the financial system as a whole. This reporting generally should include private credit funds’ connections to private equity funds, insurance companies, and other nonbank institutions; credit lines that private credit funds have with regulated banks; and basic information about the funds’ loans to private companies. This reporting should be required of all private credit funds regardless of size or structure, but the details and process could be scaled depending on the size of the fund. In particular, Congress should require more extensive information from the larger private credit funds—for example, those with assets of $10 billion or more. Finally, as they do with traditional banks, financial regulators should be required to report to Congress on a regular basis their assessment of private credit risks beyond those directly connected to traditional banks.

While bank regulators have monitored risks faced by individual institutions since the 1860s, the 2010 Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act established the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) to identify and reduce risks across the financial system. As private markets, including private credit funds, continue to grow, the potential is growing for financial regulators to develop blind spots.

The Federal Reserve regularly researches and monitors data on many aspects of the financial system and creates financial accounts—a set of statistics that tracks the flow of money through the economy, including who holds that money. These statistics are released quarterly. As the financial system becomes more complex, the Fed must update these accounts to avoid any gaps that are created in its map of the financial system.

U.S. bank loans to nondepository financial institutions—or shadow banks—had grown to $1.2 trillion as of June 2025, about $300 billion of which was to private credit providers, which include private credit and private equity funds that in turn make loans to private companies—up from about $10 billion in 2013. Those private fund borrowers are interconnected with other private equity firms, insurance companies, and asset managers. As more capital flows into these funds and more private company debt migrates to these darker corners of the financial system, private credit funds’ underwriting standards may be deteriorating. The FSOC reported that default rates among companies that have received private credit loans totaled 5.5 percent in the second quarter of 2025, compared with 3.8 percent and 1.3 percent for leveraged loans and high-yield bonds, respectively.

Because loans are often a bank’s largest asset class, default by borrowers or counterparties is perhaps the greatest risk that most banks face. Thus, they are required to provide important information on a quarterly basis in call reports to financial regulators about their assets and liabilities, which include the loans they make and receive. The Federal Reserve includes the information in these call reports in the data it uses to create the financial accounts for monitoring financial stability.

In 2026, the Federal Reserve revised their financial accounts to better integrate private credit. They used data obtained from a new federal requirement as of the fourth quarter of 2024 for banks to include private credit they have extended in aggregate reporting to regulators on loans to shadow banks. But disaggregated details about private credit loans are not required to be provided in these disclosures. Moreover, the other sources of the data the Fed uses also may not be reliable or complete. p: _본 기사는 사모대출 리스크를 다룬 3부작 시리즈의 마지막 편이다. 1편에서는 사모대출을 설명하고, 비상장 BDC(business development company) 형태로 구조화된 사모대출 펀드에 투자하는 개인투자자들이 직면한 리스크를 짚었다. 2편에서는 시야를 사모대출 펀드 전반으로 넓혀 은퇴 저축자, 퇴직연금(annuity)과 보험상품 보유자, 그리고 금융시스템에 미치는 리스크를 살폈다. 이번 글은 의회와 규제당국이 사모대출의 리스크를 줄이기 위해 취할 수 있는 조치를 제안한다._

미국의 최근 금융 역사는 규제당국이 위기가 터질 때까지 기다리지 말고 리스크가 쌓이는 단계에서 이를 더 일찍 포착해 대응해야 한다는 교훈을 준다. 사모대출 펀드와 BDC(business development company)에서 커지는 리스크를 더 잘 포착하고 금융시스템과 그 참여자들을 보호하기 위해 의회와 규제당국이 취해야 할 조치는 많다. 여기에는 고용주 후원 연금이나 401(k) 플랜에 가입한 미국인, 보험사의 퇴직연금이나 보험상품을 보유한 사람, 전통적인 은행에 돈을 맡긴 사람들에 대한 보호도 포함된다.
사모대출을 비롯한 사모 투자, 즉 대체투자는 대부분의 401(k) 플랜에서 제외하거나 극히 제한된 선택지로만 남겨 두어야 한다. 또한 Trump 행정부가 제안한 세이프 하버(safe harbor) 없이, 투자 플랜 운용자와 자문사가 신의성실 의무 위반에 대해 온전히 책임을 져야 한다.

고용주가 제공하는 퇴직저축 플랜은 내국세입법(Internal Revenue Code) 401(k)조에 따라 특별한 세제 혜택을 받는데, 이는 미국인의 노후 대비 저축을 장려한다는 공공정책을 촉진하기 위해 만들어졌다. 401(k)에 납입된 급여는 은퇴 후 근로자에게 지급될 때까지 과세되지 않으며, 고용주 역시 근로자의 401(k)에 매칭 기여금을 제공하면 공제를 받는 등 세제 혜택을 누린다. 이처럼 401(k)는 연방정부가 다른 정부 프로그램과 지출의 재원이 되었을 세금을 포기함으로써 근로자와 고용주 모두에게 납세자가 보조하는 혜택을 제공하는 셈이다.

의회는 개인투자자를 포함해 비상장 중소·중견기업에 자본 투자를 촉진하기 위해 BDC를 명시적으로 만들었다. 2026년 2분기 기준 대형 BDC들의 부채 투자 중 10%에 가까운 비중이 부실 차주와 관련돼 있었고, 이들 포트폴리오 기업에 대한 대출의 가치평가는 은행과 투자회사 등으로부터 의문이 제기돼 왔다. 따라서 BDC 투자는 통상 고위험이어서 대부분의 401(k) 플랜에는 적합하지 않다. 그 밖의 사모대출 펀드와 사모펀드(private equity) 및 기타 사모 자산 역시 투명성이 충분하지 않고 정의상 공개적으로 거래되지 않으므로 시장 규율의 적용을 받지 않는다. 이런 고위험 투자를 401(k)에 허용하면 납세자가 보조하는 저축에 정당화되기 어려운 리스크를 들여오고 미국인 은퇴자산의 금융 안정성을 훼손함으로써 납세자의 돈을 낭비하는 결과를 낳을 수 있다.

사모대출 펀드 지분이 적격투자자이든, 주법상 적합한 투자자이든, 둘 다 아니든 일반 투자자에게 판매될 때는 해당 펀드가 이들에게 충분하고 공정한 공시를 제공해야 한다. 그러한 공시에는 사모대출 펀드가 대출해 주는 기업의 가치평가에 대한 더 세부적이고 검증 가능한 내용과 이를 뒷받침하는 데이터, 그리고 포트폴리오 기업의 수, 업종, 재무 상태에 관한 데이터가 포함되어야 한다. 또한 성과보수(incentive fee)를 포함해 투자자에게 부과되는 수수료도 전부 공시해야 하는데, 수수료가 수익을 잠식할 수 있기 때문이다. 지분 환매에 대한 모든 제한 역시 투자자에게 명확히 공시하고 설명해야 한다.

미국 증권거래위원회(SEC)는 상장 BDC는 물론 비상장 BDC에도 이러한 공시 중 상당수를 요구하지만, 사모 BDC와 그 밖의 사모대출 펀드에는 같은 요구를 하지 않는다. 그런데 후자는 Regulation D나 기타 증권 공모 면제 규정을 활용해, 일부는 적격투자자(accredited investor)에도 해당하지 않는 일반 투자자에게 지분을 판매하면서도 공모를 공개 등록하거나 공개 보고서를 제출할 필요가 없다. 그러나 이들 역시 적격투자자를 포함한 일반 투자자에게 지분을 판매할 때는 공개 등록 및 공시 규정을 준수해야 한다. 한 가지 방법은 상장 BDC처럼 모든 사모대출 펀드가 일반 투자자에게 지분을 판매할 때마다 Form N-2의 제출 요건을 준수하도록 하는 것이다. 또는 이러한 공시가 있더라도 펀드 지분이 공개 거래되지 않아 일반 투자자가 통상 의지하는 가격 발견(price discovery)이 이뤄지지 않는 만큼, 이들 사모대출 펀드가 일반 투자자에게 지분을 판매하는 것을 아예 금지하는 방안도 합리적일 것이다.
보험사와 관련해서는, 주 보험규제당국이 보험사의 자본 요건 산정에 쓰이는 사모 신용등급(private credit rating)의 공개를 요구할 수 있다. 이를 통해 시장의 집단 지성을 활용해, 보험사가 투자한 사모대출 펀드 포트폴리오의 가치평가를 점검할 수 있다.

공시는 미국 증권법의 초석이다. 1933년 증권법(Securities Act of 1933)은 증권을 공모하는 회사가 해당 증권과 그 투자에 따르는 리스크에 대해 충분하고 공정한 공시를 제공하도록 요구한다. 마찬가지로 1934년 증권거래법(Securities Exchange Act of 1934)은 증권이 공개 시장에서 거래되는 회사에 지속적이고 정기적인 보고를 요구한다. 이러한 시장 투명성은 투자자가 건전한 투자 결정을 내리도록 돕고, 다른 시장 참여자가 리스크를 가격에 반영할 수 있게 하며, 공공 당국이 증권 사기를 단속하는 데도 도움이 된다.

2025년 일부 사모대출 포트폴리오 기업의 디폴트는 사모대출 펀드가 제시한 가치평가를 신뢰할 수 있는지, 펀드가 충분한 실사를 수행했는지 등 사모대출 투자의 질에 대한 투자자들의 우려를 촉발했다. 또한 인공지능(AI)의 급속한 발전으로 소프트웨어 기업들이 위협에 직면하면서, 이들 기업에 대한 사모대출 펀드 대출의 향방을 둘러싼 우려도 제기됐다. 소프트웨어 기업에 대한 대출 상당수가 지금부터 2029년 사이에 만기가 도래해 리파이낸싱이 필요하다는 점이 이런 우려를 더욱 키운다.

연기금 운용자, 401(k) 플랜의 운용자와 수탁자 및 이들이 고용한 컨설턴트, 보험사의 투자 담당자는 모두 적격투자자에 해당하지만, 의회는 이들 모두에게 건전한 의사결정을 위한 충분한 정보가 필요하며 그 결정이 이들에게 저축을 맡긴 수백만 미국인에게 영향을 미친다는 점을 인식해야 한다. 의회는 또한 일부 경우 투자자문사의 전략이 자신이 운용하는 퇴직연금 플랜의 가입자나 연금(annuity)을 운용하는 은퇴자에게 리스크를 초래할 수 있다는 점도 유념해야 한다. 사모대출 시장이 성장하고 연기금과 보험사가 이들 펀드에 더 공격적으로 투자할수록, 평범한 미국인의 저축이 걸린 투자 결정이 투명성 부족과 그 안에 감춰진 리스크로부터 보호되도록 투명성이 필요하다.
오늘날 금융시스템의 복잡성과 상호연결성, 그리고 대체로 불투명한 사모 시장의 성장을 고려하면, 금융규제당국이 금융시스템 내 신용 리스크의 그물망을 감시하기가 점점 더 어려워지고 있다. 전통적인 은행과 사모대출 펀드 모두 금융규제당국이 이러한 리스크를 감시하는 데 필요한 정보를 제공할 책임이 있어야 한다.

금융규제당국이 금융시스템의 리스크를 평가할 때 활용하는 자료 중 하나가 은행의 분기별 콜리포트(call report)다. 은행은 자신이 대출해 주는 사모대출 펀드에 대해 더 상세한 정보를 제공해야 한다. 여기에는 해당 펀드의 대출 포트폴리오에 관한 정보와, 펀드의 주요 투자자에 대한 은행의 대출을 포함해 은행이 사모대출 펀드와 맺고 있는 그 밖의 직간접적 연결고리가 포함된다.
